(Today through Saturday)...
Issued at 249 AM EDT Sun Sep 13 2026

A subtle frontal boundary will slip through the area today with a 
small threat for showers as cold advection strengthens in the 
immediate postfrontal airmass. Strong high pressure will expand 
across the Ohio Valley tonight and Monday with a brief shot of 
cooler and drier air. 

Upper ridging will expand back north into the region by Tuesday with 
a resumption of hot and humid conditions through midweek as a 
frontal boundary becomes quasi-stationary over the lower Great 
Lakes. Rain and thunderstorm chances will largely be confined to the 
northern half of Indiana late Tuesday and Wednesday before expanding 
across the area Thursday as the ridge retrogrades and enables the 
boundary to come south. Cooler temperatures are expected by late 
next weekend with continued chances for showers and storms.

Today through Monday Night

Muggy...stagnant airmass over the region early this morning under 
clear skies and light winds. Patchy fog has developed with abundant 
moisture in the near surface layer. 06Z temperatures ranged from the 
upper 60s to the mid 70s.

Fog will be the primary focus through daybreak with further 
expansion of current fog likely through daybreak under ideal 
radiational cooling conditions. Any fog will burn off quickly after 
sunrise with a mainly sunny start to the day.

A subtle frontal boundary will drift quietly through the forecast 
area during the first half of the day highlighted primarily by a 
wind shift and an increase in clouds into the early afternoon. The 
approach of a strong Canadian high pressure diving out of the 
northern Plains will create a sharpening baroclinic zone in the 
immediate postfrontal environment which will strengthen cold 
advection across the forecast area by late day and bring a 3-5 hour 
period with breezy northwest winds. Scattered convection may break 
out by late afternoon in the vicinity of the boundary but this will 
be focused primarily to the east of the area across Ohio where model 
soundings show steeper lapse rates through about 600mb and modest 
instability. Any rain for the forecast area likely comes in the form 
of showers or possibly a rumble of thunder associated with the 
baroclinic zone late afternoon and early evening before diminishing 
near sunset.  

The aforementioned high will swing through the Great Lakes tonight 
and Monday with a notable area of deep subsidence pivoting across 
the northeast half of the forecast area. This will aid in a 
spectacular day Monday highlighted by sunny skies...much lower 
humidity levels and cooler temperatures. Diurnal cu will be limited 
to the lower Wabash Valley primarily where afternoon humidity levels 
will be subtly higher. As the high moves into New England and takes 
the subsidence east of the region Monday night...return flow will 
develop quickly with gradual moisture advection aloft back across 
the Ohio Valley by early Tuesday.

Temps...highs in the mid and upper 80s will be common by the 
afternoon but the increase in cold advection and a drop in dewpoints 
will bring a refreshing feel to the air over the northern half of 
the forecast area by late day. Low level thermals on Monday support 
highs ranging from the mid 70s northeast to the lower 80s in the 
lower Wabash Valley. Lows tonight will fall into the 50s over much 
of the area then recovering back into the lower and mid 60s Monday 
night.

Tuesday through Sunday

The expansion of the upper ridge back into the Tennessee Valley 
combined with strengthening S/SW flow will draw higher dewpoint air 
back into the Ohio Valley with hot and humid conditions returning 
Tuesday and Wednesday. A cold front will shift across the upper 
Midwest and into the Great Lakes on Tuesday as deep low pressure 
moves to near James Bay but any further southward progression to the 
boundary  will be stopped there with the strong ridge in place to 
the south and the western part of the front becoming nearly parallel 
to the mean flow aloft. There remains potential for the boundary to 
get close enough to the area Tuesday night and Wednesday morning for 
more organized convection to impact mainly the northern half of the 
forecast area. This will be temporary as the retrogression of the 
upper ridge leads to height rises back into the central Plains and 
subsequently pushes the boundary back to the north on Wednesday.

Beyond Wednesday...extended guidance begins to deviate in the 
handling of just how quickly heights aloft buckle in response to the 
center of the upper ridge drifting west into the Southern Plains. 
This will be aided by a sharp upper wave traversing across southern 
Canada but uncertainty remains with regards to how far south into or 
through the forecast area that the frontal boundary can make it.
